column4: Subject M: embedded directly in the sample tube; small rotations between some sections and gouging in the last third
column5: For subject M, we embedded directly in the sample tube using 2% agarose gel. Due to insufficient surface area to glue the tissue to the plunger, during imaging of subject M we observed small rotations between some sections. Additionally, there was some tissue gouging in the last third of subject M due to gel softness and degradation

column4: sagittal mold embedding test: no rotational misalignment but cracking during sectioning
column5: Tissue was embedded in the sagittal position using a silicone mold as shown in Figure 2b with 4% agarose gel. ... This eliminated rotational misalignment. However the increased gel stiffness caused cracking during sectioning

column4: 3.25% wt low-melting-point agarose, heated to 140 °C until clear, kept at ≥ 40 °C
column5: For Subject V, 400 ml of 3.25% wt low-melting-point agarose gel solution was prepared by heating to 140 °C under a constant stir until clear. It was kept at a minimum of 40 °C to maintain the liquid state prior to use

column4: approximately; stage 1: warm liquid agarose injected with a blunt needleless syringe into the cerebellum-occipital gap; central sulcus; interhemispheric fissure
column5: a blunt, needleless syringe was used to inject approximately 100 ml of warm, liquid agarose gel into areas difficult to penetrate with submersion, including the space between the cerebellum and the occipital lobe, the central sulcus, and the interhemispheric fissure

column4: stage 2: silicone mold in an incubator so the gel penetrates the brain; cooled to room temperature before demolding
column5: The mold was placed inside an incubator set to 40 °C for 60 minutes, allowing the gel to penetrate the brain

column4: additional agarose for the specimen-tube pour; kept at 100 °C until poured
column5: An additional 500 ml of agarose gel was prepared for stage 3 (Fig. 2c) and kept at 100 °C until poured

column4: flat gel surface glued to the compresstome plunger; then the tube filled with agarose; gel surface sectioned until tissue visible
column5: The embedded sample was attached to the plunger of the compresstome with a cyanoacrylate glue applied to the flat surface of the gel. After allowing 5-10 minutes for the glue to cure, the additional agarose was carefully poured around the sample to fill the specimen tube

column4: custom specimen tube; stated to fit a whole human brain hemisphere
column5: With a 120 mm diameter and 175 mm depth, our custom compresstome can accommodate a sample as large as a whole human brain hemisphere

column4: custom specimen tube
column5: With a 120 mm diameter and 175 mm depth

column4: Lytron Kodiak series recirculating chiller; implemented between Subject M and Subject V

column5: Slice quality and sample integrity improved with these changes, which were implemented between Subject M and Subject V. Sections were collected intact from the imaging bath and placed into long-term storage

column2: 4% PFA mixed with hydrogel monomer solution (HMS)
column4: perfused; fixed overnight; washed; stored in 10% PBS; variable days to imaging (dMRI in between), no significant impact
column5: Brains were intracardially exsanguinated and perfused with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA). The PFA was mixed with hydrogel monomer solution (HMS), as described in Xu et al., 2021, to facilitate later histology. After extraction, brains were fixed overnight, washed, and stored in 10% PBS until imaging
